SECTION I:  PLAN SUMMARY
A. Goals for the The primary goal of this open space and recreation plan is to protect the natural resources
of the City and to ensure that sufficient recreational opportunities are available to all of
Woburn's citizens.
The major goals of the open space and recreation plan are:
•
Provide active and passive recreational opportunities for all residents
•
Manage existing recreation and conservation lands for maximum benefits
•
Protect Woburn's natural resources
•
Acquire new open space lands
•
Consider regional connections in open space planning efforts
•
Protect cultural and historic resources
B. Major Recommendations
The two key recommendations of the plan are:
•
To undertake management actions that will ensure a more balanced use of
conservation areas to avoid overcrowding and impacts on sensitive
environmental areas.
•
To continue to upgrade existing parks to meet the recreational needs of all
residents.

This page intentionally left blank

SECTION II:  INTRODUCTION
A. Statement of Purpose
The purpose of this open space and recreation plan is to protect the natural resources of
the City of Woburn, and to ensure that sufficient recreational opportunities are available to
all of Woburn's citizens.
B. The protection of natural resources is critical to ensuring that sufficient water is
available for the continued residential and economic growth of the community, and to
providing an environment that balances development with natural areas.  The provision of
recreational opportunities is critical to creating a community that is a desirable place to live
and work.  Because there is limited land remaining and limited financial resources, this
plan will ensure that wise, cost-effective decisions are made in the future.
Since 2002, EOEEA has been implementing an Environmental Justice Policy to help
ensure that all Massachusetts residents experience equal protection and meaningful
involvement with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of
environmental laws, regulations, and policies and the equitable distribution of
environmental benefits.  This policy was instituted recognizing that communities across
the Commonwealth, particularly those densely populated urban neighborhoods in and
around the Commonwealth's older industrial areas, are facing many environmental
challenges associated with Massachusetts' industrial legacy.  Residents in these
predominantly low-income and minority communities - nearly 29% of the
Commonwealth's population - lack open space and recreational resources and often live
side-by-side numerous existing large and small sources of pollution and old abandoned,
contaminated sites, which can pose risks to public health and the environment
(Commonwealth of Massachusetts, Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs,
Division of Conservation Services, 2008).
Critical to advancing environmental justice (EJ) in the Commonwealth is the equitable
distribution of environmental assets such as parks, open space, and recreation. Toward
this end, and where applicable, municipalities shall identify and prioritize open space sites
in their Open Space and Recreation Plans that are socially, recreationally, and ecologically
important to EJ populations within the community.
The City of Woburn has 17,665 people living in the environmental justice block groups
which represent 44.8% of the population in the City (MassGIS, 2022). EJ neighborhoods'
status is based on the percentages set by the Commonwealth for characteristics of race
and ethnicity, income, and English isolation.

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts considers a community to be an environmental
justice community if it meets one or more of the following criteria (MassGIS, 2022):
• The annual median household income is 65 percent or less of the statewide
annual median household income
• Minorities make up 40 percent or more of the population
• 25 percent or more of households identify as speaking English less than
"very well"
• Minorities make up 25 percent of the population and the annual median
household income of the municipality in which the neighborhood is located
does not exceed 150 percent of the statewide annual median household
income
C. Planning Process and Public Participation
The first step in the process of writing the plan was to schedule two kick-off Public
Workshops and publicize an online survey to solicit input from residents. A third Public
Workshop was held to report back on input received from the first two Public Workshops as
well as the online survey and to ask attendees to prioritize the Action Items compiled through
the public process. Further details on the public participation process are provided in
Section VI.
The workshops and online survey were advertised extensively through email blasts, social
media posts, and website updates. The workshops and survey availability were also
announced at in-person public meetings of the Planning Board on August 23, 2022,
September 13, 2022, and October 11, 2022.  They were also mentioned at a meeting of
the Woburn Redevelopment Authority on September 27, 2022.  All of these meetings were
broadcast live and repeatedly re-aired afterward on Woburn's local cable television station.
The workshops and survey were also discussed at in-person meetings of the Recreation
Department held at City Hall on September 8, 2022, October 6, 2022, November 3, 2022
and December 1, 2022.   Discussion about the draft Plan was a specific agenda topic at
each of these four Commission meetings, the agendas for which were all posted on the
City Clerk's bulletin board in advance of the meetings as required by the Open Meeting
Law.   Notices of the workshops were mailed out to local Housing Authority residents.
Finally, paper notices of the workshops/survey availability were posted on public bulletin
boards outside the Recreation and Planning Department offices at City Hall, at Spence
Farm, at the main Library and the Senior Center, and at Spring Court Extension, a Housing
Authority-managed property in close proximity to the project.
The electronic outreach efforts and communication included the following:

• Email blasts were sent to Woburn recreation patrons and residents to inform them
about upcoming workshops and the online survey.
• Email templates were created for Woburn Housing Authority to inform residents
about upcoming workshops and the online survey.
• Social media prompts and graphics were produced to promote the survey and
workshops on Facebook and Twitter.
• Workshop notices and surveys were posted on the City's municipal and Recreation
Department website.
Public participation and outreach results are summarized in Appendix A.

SECTION III:  COMMUNITY SETTING
A. Regional Context
The City of Woburn, 12.94 square miles in area, is located in Middlesex County and is
bordered by six communities: Wilmington on the north, Reading and Stoneham on the
east, Winchester on the south, Lexington on the southwest, and Burlington on the west.
Woburn is a suburban industrial city located along the upper Mystic River valley,
approximately ten miles from Boston, sixteen miles from Lowell, and eleven miles from
Waltham.
1) Subregion - Woburn is a member of the North Suburban Planning Council (NSPC),
one of eight MAPC subregions.  The North Suburban Planning Council is a group of
nine communities (Burlington, Lynnfield, North Reading, Reading, Stoneham,
Wakefield, Wilmington, Winchester and Woburn) that meet regularly to discuss
issues of common interest. The North Suburban Planning Council is an excellent
forum for discussing regional open space issues and opportunities.  The only
community abutting Woburn that is not a member of NSPC is Lexington.  For more
information on the North Suburban Planning Council, please go to www.mapc.org
and visit the page for the subregions.
2) MetroCommon 2050 - MetroCommon 2050 is the official regional plan for Greater
Boston, adopted consistent with the requirements of Massachusetts General Laws
(MetroCommon 2050).   The plan includes myriad goals falling within five general
topic areas:  Inclusive Growth and Mobility; Homes for Everyone; Equity of Wealth &
Health; Dynamic and Representative Government; and Climate Change Mitigation
and Resiliency.  Woburn's Open Space and Recreation Plan contains a number of
goals and projects that are consistent with strategies and recommendations
contained in MetroCommon 2050, including the following:
• Goal A.   Getting Around The Region:  Traveling around Metro Boston is safe,
affordable, convenient, and enjoyable.   Woburn's Open Space and Recreation
Plan recognizes the City's concerted effort to create multi-use paths across the
City that expand Woburn's walking and biking network and provide access to
open spaces and other uses.
• Goal F.  Greater Boston's air, water, land, and other natural resources are clean
and protected - for us and for the rest of the ecosystem.  This Plan calls for
improving, augmenting, and connecting existing parks, open space and
greenways across the City to preserve wildlife habitat and safeguard the
environment in ways that also provide enjoyable recreational opportunities.

• Goal I.  Healthy and Safe Neighborhoods:  We are safe, healthy, and connected
to one another.   Woburn's Plan includes a detailed list of potential State, Federal
and private funding sources to augment City funds to ensure the goals and
objectives laid out in the Plan are realistically affordable.
3) Regional projects - There are two major regional projects: the Middlesex Canal and
the Tri-Community Bikeway/Greenway.
Middlesex Canal - The Middlesex Canal was a 27-mile-long waterway that connected
Boston to the Merrimack River in Lowell.  The canal carried freight and passengers from
1803 to 1853 and played an important role in the development of the communities north of
Boston.  The Middlesex Canal Commission has been active in preserving and restoring
the canal.  The Commission has received federal funding to undertake a phased
restoration of the canal.  The goal of the Commission is to restore the canal to provide for
boating, walking, biking and other recreational opportunities along the canal towpath.
Tri-Community Bikeway/Greenway - The Tri-Community Bikeway/Greenway was
constructed in 2018.  The project is a 5.7-mile multi-use path connecting portions of
Stoneham, Winchester, and Woburn. The path begins at Recreation Park near the center
of Stoneham and follows an abandoned Boston and Maine Railroad right-of-way north
past the Middle School and then southwest over Main Street to an existing underpass at I93. It continues west through Woburn under I-93 following the railroad right-of-way and
then southwest along Washington Street to Winchester. The path follows the Aberjona
River corridor southwest with a new crossing under the commuter rail line near the Muraco
School.  It continues south into Winchester Center passing within a short block of the
commuter rail station.  The route continues south paralleling the commuter rail line and
connects directly to the Wedgemere commuter rail station.  Another segment of the path is
located along the north and south shoreline of Horn Pond in Woburn.  The existing Horn
Pond Brook bike path in Winchester links the south end of this segment to the segment
described above.
1. History of the Community
Woburn was founded by a group of seven Charlestown residents in the early 1640's who
decided to establish a new town.  The settlement included the land area that is now the
towns of Wilmington, Burlington, and Winchester.   Incorporated in 1642, the first general
town meeting was held in 1643; at the time, absence from a town meeting without an
excuse meant a fine of 18 pence.

As the town's location on the Aberjona and Horn Pond Rivers fueled industrial growth, the
first school house was built in 1713 and by the 1740's the City's population had grown to
1,400.  Industry continued to grow, , largely because of the abundant water supply and
transportation networks afforded by the Aberjona River and the Middlesex Canal, the
country's first regional transportation canal, opened in 1803. Shortly thereafter, the Boston
and Lowell Railroad opened in 1835, helping to establish Woburn as a manufacturing
center.  The
By 1800 there were 156 dwellings and 22 shoe shops, 2 currying shops, 3 sawmills and 7
grist mills operating in the town.  The Middlesex Canal, The first major industry was shoe
and boot manufacturing, and in fact, during the King Philip's Wars, the town taxes were
partially paid in shoes.  By the 1860's, the production of leather had become the town's
primary industry.  In 1865, 300 men and women worked in Woburn tanneries which
shipped $1.7 million worth of leather across the country.  Woburn was at the head of the
tanning industry in the country by then, attracting immigrants from Ireland, Nova Scotia
and other parts of Canada to work in the tanneries.  By 1884, 26 large tanneries employed
1,500 men and women and produced $4.5 million worth of leather.  The ability to transport
materials and goods via the waterways and railroad enabled the tanning, shoemaking,
and other industries to thrive.
Public telephones came to Woburn in 1882 and electric lights in 1885.  Woburn was
incorporated as a city in 1889; by 1892, its population had reached 14,000 and there were
about 2,300 dwellings in the City, 197 streets totaling about 63 miles of roadway, and 48
schools serving over 2,500 students.
The early 1900's was a period of growth and development.  Woburn's first sewer system
was operational by 1905, a new High School was built in 1906, its first hospital in 1909 and
post office in 1911.  By 1915 Woburn's business economy had diversified.  Factories were
making ice cream, machine tools, mops, and paper boxes among other goods, and the
leather tanning industry continued alongside them.  Like much of the region, Woburn's
manufacturing industry underwent periodic stagnation in the 1900's, especially during the
Great Depression. And yet, continued expansion of transportation infrastructure spurred
additional growth.
The City's population has steadily grown to 41,000, and it retains a healthy base of
industrial and commercial uses of all kinds, including office space, life sciences and
biotechnology uses, and medical facilities.

which represent 44.8% of the population in the City (MassGIS, 2022). Commonwealth of
Massachusetts considers a community to be an environmental justice community if it
meets one or more of the following criteria:

• The annual median household income is 65 percent or less of the statewide
annual median household income
• Minorities make up 40 percent or more of the population
• 25 percent or more of households identify as speaking English less than
"very well"
• Minorities make up 25 percent of the population and the annual median

does not exceed 150 percent of the statewide annual median household

The City of Woburn consists of EJ population with minority criteria (yellow census block
groups) and minority and income criteria (dark green block groups) (see Figure 2:
Environmental Justice Populations and map on page 12) (MA Executive Office of Energy
and Environmental Affairs, 2022). Over 9.6% of the community in Woburn is Asian, the
City's largest minority group (U.S. Census 2021). In the 2021 ACS 4.8% of respondents
reported their ethnicity as Black or African American alone and 6.2% as Hispanic or Latino.
The median household income in Woburn is $95,184, which is less than neighboring
communities of Burlington ($124,755), Lexington ($202,852), Reading ($145,552),
Stoneham ($105,541), Wilmington ($146,250), and Winchester ($184,844). Around 6.4% of
residents in Woburn are living in poverty and around 12% of Woburn residents have a
disability (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021). Investment in parks can provide these
demographics with increased accessibility, reduction in flooding and urban heat island
effect, and improved air quality. A review of Figure 2: Environmental Justice Populations
reveals that EJ block groups northwest of Route 128/I-95 have less access to parks than
other EJ block groups. This portion of the City may benefit from additional investment in
parks.

D. Growth and Development Patterns
1. Patterns and trends
Chosen for it's location on the Aberjona and Horn Pond Rivers, the Town of Woburn was
settled in the early 1640's and primarily an agricultural community. The two rivers offered
both a means of transportation and sanitation, and the surrounding hills, protection.  Most
industries were sited on the waterways which were used as a source of power. The first
tanning enterprise started in 1648 near the Common. Shoe making shops began to
appear in the late 1600s, and more small tanneries appeared.   Although agriculture
remained the foundation of the economy until the 1800s, David Cummings established a
large-scale tanning operation in 1756, a foreshadowing of the town's later dependence on
the leather processing industry. The development of transportation facilities and its
proximity to Boston helped to establish Woburn as a shoe and boot manufacturing center.
Most land uses in the 19th century were in support of the growing shoe and boot
manufacturing industry and included grist mills, shoe shops, curing shops and residential
dwellings.  As Woburn's factories produced diversified goods, growth continued into the
1900's, necessitating expanded infrastructure and support services such as a sanitary
sewer system, schools and hospitals.  By 1940 the City's population was almost 20,000
and that jumped to over 31,000 by 1960, due in no small part to the fact that Route 128
opened for service in 1951.  The Woburn section of Interstate I-93 opened in 1960, further
spurring additional residential development and business growth throughout the City.
Over the past 50 years, Woburn has become less of an industrial center and more of a
commercial business and residential community.   It dealt with significant environmental
conditions that harkened back to not only its history with the leather industry but also with
the chemical and metalworking industries that followed. The Woburn of today is mix of
quiet residential neighborhoods whose homes reflect virtually all of the residential
architectural styles, vibrant office and industrial parks, and wooded conservation areas,
such as the Horn Pond Reservation, Forest Park, and Shaker Glen. Several areas of the
City are now being reshaped into compact, mixed-use districts where modern housing
and commercial amenities exist side-by-side near major highways and the rail service that
connects Woburn with Boston and points North as far as Maine.

2. Infrastructure
a. Transportation
Woburn has excellent access through two major highways: I-93 and Route 128 (I-95). The
interchange of these two major highways lies just east of Woburn in the Town of Reading.
The major local roads providing north-south access are Main Street (Route 38),
Cambridge Street (Route 3), and Washington Street. The major east-west routes are
Lexington Street, Montvale Avenue and Salem Street. Traffic congestion is a serious
problem in Woburn.
There is one location in Woburn (Montvale Avenue and Albany Street) that was on the
Massachusetts Highway Department's list of top 200 intersection crash locations for 20102012. In 2022, the City completed the Montvale Ave. widening, which has mitigated traffic
congestion in the area. This project was funded through the Transportation Improvements
Program.

The City is currently in the process of constructing the New Boston St. Bridge over the
Commuter Rail line. Once completed, the bridge will connect New Boston Street to the
north and south. This link will provide a commercial beltway connecting Commerce Way,
Mishawum Rd., Industrial Way, New Boston St. and Presidential Way. This critical
transportation node will relieve traffic congestion by allowing multiple paths for vehicular
traffic to gain access to both Route 93 and 95. The Bridge is expected to trigger
redevelopment of single story commercial/industrial buildings into mixed use housing and
retail facilities.
The City completed the Tri-Community Bikeway along the former B&M Railroad from
Winchester to Stoneham in 2018. In conjunction with the City's Complete Streets Program,
opportunities to provide better bike accommodations have been identified or
implementation. The City has received a grant from MassTrails to design segments 2 and
3 of a Rail Trail multi modal path from Wilmington to Library Field in the downtown. This
work resulted from the Bikeway Feasibility study performed in 2021.
In addition to the pedestrian benefits of the Bikeway and Rail Trail projects, seven of the
City's nine zoning overlay districts (listed on page 25) are intended to promote mixed-use
developments to improve the city's walkability.
The City is in the process of designing the Downtown Traffic Improvements Project that will
mitigate traffic congestion and vehicular accidents in the downtown area. This project is
TIP funded and is programmed for construction in 2025.
Commuter rail service to North Station in Boston is currently available at the Anderson
Regional Transportation Center. This center includes a new commuter rail station, highway
interchange and Park and Ride facility. The City has a second commuter rail station at
Mishawum which is now on a reduced schedule designed to provide reverse commute
service from Boston to local businesses.
Bus service is also provided to the City by the MBTA with trips to Boston and surrounding
communities.
b. Water Supply Systems
The City of Woburn has operated a public water system beginning in 1871 when the State
passed enabling legislation for the construction of a water pumping station, a reservoir
and a distribution system. The City obtains its water supply from the Horn Pond Well Field
and the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority.
Improvements to the well field included the replacement of the original Well D in 2005 with
Well D2, situated approximately 50 feet to the north. Well D2 is the newest of the Horn
Pond well houses and like the other four active Horn Pond Wells, it has a variable
frequency drive and ground water observation wells with depth transducers. The SCADA
(Scheduled Control and Data Acquisition) system, located at the Groundwater Treatment

Facility, monitors the ground water level in the wells and automatically decreases the
speed of the pump motor if the ground water elevation approaches the top of the well
screens, thus protecting the wells from over drafting. All of the wells are equipped with this
feature and the well production is adjusted on a continuous basis to meet daily demands.
The Horn Pond Well Field is capable of producing up to 4 MGD. The balance of the city's
6.5 MGD average daily demand is obtained from the MWRA through meters 200 and 230.
In 2012, Meter 230 and its underground vault were replaced with a new pressure reducing
valve and an above ground building. The MWRA is in the process of constructing a
redundant water supply line through Stoneham and Reading which will connect at Meter
230 and increase the reliability of the MWRA supply. These two supply sources are
expected to serve the needs of the community well into the future.
There are over 190 miles of water mains, ranging in size from 6 inch to 24 inch that
distribute water throughout the City. There are approximately 80 miles of unlined cast iron
pipe main installed between 1912 and 1928, with approximately 30 miles of cement lined
transit pipe installed throughout the late 1960's and early 1970's. The remaining 80 miles
of main consists of cement lined ductile iron pipe. Since 2000, the City has cleaned and
lined approximately 34 miles of old cast iron main and replaced another 89 miles of cast
iron main with larger ductile iron main. The City appropriated another $6 million in 2014 to
continue its annual capital program of cleaning and lining or replacing unlined cast iron
water mains from the early 1900's. In conjunction with the cleaning and lining effort, the
City has replaced over 500 hydrants and 1,100 gate valves. The cleaning and lining effort
has reduced water quality issues associated with discolored water as well as reducing
unaccounted for water associated with the lead and oakum joints of the older cast iron
mains.
There are four major service areas within the distributions system. The low service area is
maintained by the Rag Rock Storage Tank and the supply sources. The West side high
service area is supplied by the Shaker Glenn Booster Pump Station and storage is
provided in the Whispering Hill Tank. There are two pumps to demand service areas that
include Blueberry Hill and Montvale Ave. The Shaker Glenn Pump Station, constructed in
1950 was replaced in the spring of 2015 by the construction of a new 2 MGD Pump
Station.
In 2002, the City constructed the Horn Pond Corrosion Control Facility to meet the
mandated lead and copper rule. The facility provided for the adjustment of pH using
Sodium Hydroxide and the addition of poly-ortho phosphate to sequester iron and
manganese found within the groundwater supply. The sequestering agent also coats
unlined cast iron pipes to inhibit sloughing of the biofilm. The facility provides for
disinfection using sodium hypochlorite and fluoridation using hydrofluosilicic acid. All the
chemical feed dosages and well pump rates are monitored by a SCADA system
(scheduled control and data acquisition), located in the Central Control Room, to ensure
that the proper chemical concentrations are maintained on a continuous basis. The
SCADA system also monitors the system pressure, flow rate and water elevation at the two

MWRA pressure reducing valves; six booster pump stations; five municipal wells and three
storage tanks within the system. The facility includes an administrative area, laboratory,
locker rooms, electrical and mechanical rooms along with the chemical rooms.
In 2012, the treatment facility was expanded to include pressure filtration to remove iron
and manganese, which had been increasing and was the source of periodic discolored
water. The filters and media are rated for 4 MGD. The expansion included the addition of
ultraviolet disinfection as a precaution against cryptosporidium and giardia from the
influence of Horn Pond on the groundwater supply. As part of the project, a 10,000 square
foot water distribution building was constructed to house the water department personnel,
21 equipment and materials. The water distribution building contains offices, water meter
storage room, materials storage room, locker rooms and lunch area for the workers. The
architecture of both the water treatment facility and the distribution building mirror
elements of the 1871 pump station in the entrance arches, brick corbelling, granite window
sills and slate roofs, such that the water complex as a whole is historically consistent in its
appearance. Water
The City is in the process of designing a new PFAS treatment addition for the Horn Pond
Treatment facility. Construction is scheduled for the summer of 2024.Storage Facilities
The existing Rag Rock water storage tank was replaced in 2012 with a new 3.9 MG
prestressed concrete tank. The tank includes a circulation system on the influent riser that
allows better mixing of water within the tank and available chlorine remains fairly constant.
With the commissioning of the new concrete tank, the old steel tank was demolished in 2012
and the site restored as open space under the jurisdiction of the Conservation Commission.
The Rag Rock Storage Tank maintains the pressure in the Low Service Area. The Whispering
Hill tank is a pre-stressed concrete storage facility constructed in 1970 with a capacity of 4.0
MG that serves the West Side High Service Area. The Whispering Hill tank is expected to
remain in service for the foreseeable future. In addition to structured storage facilities within
the community, the city has the capability to obtain an additional 17 MGD from the MWRA
through its meter connections and there are three hardened emergency connections to
neighboring communities should the need ever arise.
c. Sewer Service
Woburn is 95 percent served by the MWRA sewer system. The MWRA's Woburn interceptor
passes along portions of Water Street, Sturgis Street and Arlington Road adjacent to the
north and east sides of Horn Pond. There are no NPDES discharges in Woburn. The City of
Woburn began collecting sewage from households and commercial entities in 1879. Today
there are over 170 miles of sewer collection facilities and interceptor lines that discharge to
the MWRA system. There are over 13,500 residential and commercial units connected to
the sewer system with approximately 400 septic systems still in service, such that 97% of
the City is currently connected to sewerage. Over the last 10 years, the City has undertaken
an aggressive program to eliminate extraneous infiltration and inflow sources from the

system This tactic has reduced the average daily sewage flow from 11.5 MGD in 2006 to
8.2 MGD in 2013.
This reduction in flow has occurred primarily in the West Woburn system tributary to Horn
Pond. This reduction in average day sewage flow has had a beneficial impact on the
sewer system overflow that occurs from the Horn Pond Interceptor off of Sturgis Street.
The frequency and duration of the overflow is far less than occurred before the system
improvements were completed. Previously, a two year rainstorm would trigger an overflow
and currently the system can confine up to a ten year storm.
The City has undertaken a seven year program to reduce infiltration and inflow in the East
Woburn system with similar results expected. There are no sewer system overflows in the
East Side tributary area; however reductions in infiltration and inflow reduce the impacts of
the MWRA sewer assessments on the City budget. The City is in it's fifth year of sewer
system rehabilitation on the east side of the City.
3. Long-term development patterns
There are sixteen zoning districts in Woburn including four residential districts and eight
commercial districts.  Figure 3 shows the zoning district boundaries.
In addition to the 16 districts listed there are nine overlay districts:
• Upper Main Street Overlay District
• Intergenerational Overlay District
• Commerce Way Corridor Overlay District
• Mishawum Station Transit Oriented Development Overlay District
• Technology & Business Mixed Use Overlap District
• Smart Growth Overlay District - Woburn Mall
• Woburn Loop Bikeway / Greenway
• Solar Overlay District
• Life Sciences District
The Woburn Loop Bikeway/Greenway Overlay District is intended to promote
redevelopment of underutilized, abandoned or obsolete industrial and commercial sites to
residential use.  The Mishawum Station Transit Oriented Development Overlay District is
designed to encourage development and redevelopment near the Mishawum commuter

rail station.  The purpose of the Intergenerational Overlay District is to provide diverse
housing options and minimize impacts on public schools. The Commerce Way Corridor
Overlay District is intended to encourage reuse of obsolete and underutilized industrial
and commercial space for mixed office, retail and multi-family uses.  The Upper Main
Street Overlay District was developed to encourage residential reuse on portions of
Woburn's Main Street.  Finally, the Solar Overlay District was enacted to promote largescale, ground-mounted solar installations across the City.
The City also has a cluster development provision.  One of the purposes of the cluster
provision is the permanent protection of open space which is of use and value to the city
and which would not otherwise be protected under regular zoning.  Another purpose of the
cluster provision is to protect natural features through creative site planning.  Cluster
development requires a special permit.  The application for a special permit must include
information on the proposed use of the open space, an evaluation of its value to the city
with respect to natural resource preservation and accessibility.   The ordinance requires
that at least 30% of the total area of a development parcel be set aside as open space and
further requires that the open space parcel  be conveyed to either the City or a
homeowners' association trust.  In either case, the open space would increase the City's
level of service by providing expanded access to recreation space or additional acreage
for conservation.

Specifically, and as detailed in Section VII, Goals and Objectives, the City should pursue:
•
complete regular maintenance and replacements of recreational assets,
• address deferred maintenance through a maintenance management plan and

SECTION IV:  ENVIRONMENTAL INVENTORY AND ANALYSIS
A. Geology, Soils and Topography
1. Topography - Woburn covers an area of 12.6 square miles.  Elevations range from 43
feet above sea level at Horn Pond to nearly 340 feet at the top of Zion Hill in west Woburn.
Woburn is hilly in the south and west, while the north and east are relatively open and flat.
2. Soils - Topography and parent rock material, along with climate and vegetation are the
major factors which influence the formation of regional soils.  The humid climate of
Massachusetts and the characteristic mixed hardwood and coniferous forests have
contributed to the production of northern gray soils classified as spodosols.  These are
typically acid soils with a strongly developed leached zone, underlain by a spodic horizon
of accumulated iron and/or organic material.  Till soils are the most abundant, followed by
outwash soils, then rough-stony soils.  With the exception of limestone-modified soils and
soils formed on alluvial and lacustrine deposits, Massachusetts soils have only low to
moderate fertility.
Woburn has two general categories of soils: rough-stony soils and till soils.  Rough-stony
soils are found predominantly in woodlands and have little or no agricultural value.  Till
soils are the most abundant and their compositions are similar to the underlying bedrock.
The soil types of Woburn are more specifically described below and are shown on Figure
5. Hollis-Millis Association:  These fine sandy loams, often very stony.  They develop in thin
deposits over the granitic bedrock and occupy approximately 35% of the City of Woburn.
Bedrock near the surface, ledge outcrops and surface stones severely limit any kind of
development if on-site sewage disposal systems must be used.
1. Hinckley-Gravel Pits - Made Land Association:  These are droughty, sandy gravely
soils that occur mostly in the eastern half of the City.  They have developed in
deeper deposits than those of the Hollis soils and provide large supplies of ground
water for community or industrial use.
2. Hinckley-Merrimac-Deerfield Association:  These are moderately to well-drained
sandy and gravely soils that occupy 15% of the City.  The Deerfield soils are heavily
used for agricultural purposes.  These soils are adequately drained when not near a
high water table and are quite productive when dewatered.
3. Canton-Hollis Association:  These are very stony, well drained soils.  They occur on
a series of low hills and narrow intervals in the southwestern half of the City.  They
have severe limitations for any kind of development but are suitable for some
recreational uses and as woodland.
4. Muck-Fresh Water Marsh-Scarboro Association:  These are poorly drained organic
and mineral soils.  They are best suited for wetland wildlife and recreation.  High
water tables and low load-bearing capacity severely limit any other use of these
soils.

A large amount of soil has been brought in from other areas and used in commercial
development.  This soil is unclassified by the Soil Conservation Service.  Wet, swampy
soils occupy lowland areas and are most predominant in the northern and eastern areas
of Woburn, such as the Aberjona River floodplain.
B. Landscape Character
Woburn is a densely developed suburb with a large employment base due to its excellent
highway access.  The southwestern portion of the city is less developed and there are still
views of fields and undeveloped spaces interspersed with residential development.  The
high points in the city such as the Rag Rock conservation area and Horn Pond Mountain
which afford sweeping views of a variety of landscapes including the Boston skyline.  The
impact of additional development will be felt most strongly in the southwestern portion of
the city as the demand for residential development continues.
C. Water Resources
The City lies within the Mystic River Watershed. There are two major catchments within the
City, The Aberjona River catchment in East Woburn and the Horn Pond catchment in West
Woburn. The groundwater fed by the Horn Pond catchment provides the City's water
supply.
Groundwater recharge areas within the City are mapped in the City's graphical information
system (GIS). These areas are protected under law by local zoning ordinance, such that
deleterious uses which could harm the aquifer are prohibited.  The groundwater recharge
area (Groundwater Protection Zone II) lies generally in the western and southcentral portions
of the City and consists of approximately 1,900 acres or a little over 20% of the City's total
land area.  It stretches from Cambridge Road near the Burlington town line east to Mount
Pleasant Street and north to Lowell Street.  A roughly 40-acre Groundwater Protection Zone
I area lies within the boundaries of the Zone II district; the Zone I area surrounds the water
treatment plant on Cove Street/Woburn Parkway where the five municipal wells are located.
The most current FEMA Floodplain Mapping is also maintained within the City GIS. Zoning
by laws exist to regulate development in and around flood prone areas. The City's All
Hazards Mitigation Plan also identifies local flood prone areas too small to be included in
the FEMA Flood Study.
The City GIS also identifies wetland resources throughout the City. These resource areas
and local floodplain fall under the jurisdiction of the Woburn Conservation Commission.
Any development in and around wetland resource areas must meet the performance

standards of MGL Chapter 131 and the Local Wetlands Ordinance. Wetlands are
scattered throughout the City, with most being small in scale.  There are virtually no
wetlands in the core of the City near the downtown, but there are clusters of larger-scale
wetlands in several places in West Woburn: (a) West and North of Hallmark Road and
Duren Avenue/Russell Street); (b) north of Wyman Street, from the Burlington line to
Middlesex Canal Park Drive; and (c) along the Burlington town line North of Route 128,
from Sylvan Road to Bartlett Drive.  There are also larger-scale areas of wetlands in East
Woburn along the entire reach of the Aberjona River and around Whittemore Pond.
The City is in the process of designing two stream, floodplain and wetland restoration
projects to mitigate flood hazards and improve water quality by enhancing the wetland
areas. One project is the 12.5 acre parcel at Shaker Glenn which will increase flood
storage, restore wetlands and create an environmental park with walking trails. The
second project is the former Hurld School Resilient Climate and Nature based Park of 11.5
acres. This project will also increase flood storage, restore wetlands and create an
environmental park with walking trails as well as a passive play park.
Seven brooks flow through Woburn:  Sucker Brook, Shaker Glen Brook, Fowl Brook, Little
Brook, Cummings Brook, Halls Brook and Horn Pond Brook.  The Aberjona River also
flows through the City.  There are several named ponds (Horn, Whittemore, Burbank,
Philips, Baltic) and several smaller, unnamed ponds.  There is also a remnant of the
Middlesex Canal that still has water in it.
1. Horn Pond - Horn Pond, located in Woburn, drains an area of about seven square
miles, primarily in Woburn and Burlington.  Horn Pond is a heavily used recreational
resource.  There is an intensively used walking path around the pond, and it is a very
popular fishing spot. Horn Pond Hill also hosts threatened species.  The pond is also
important to the water supply.  It lies within the Zone II of Woburn's water supply wells, and
there is believed to be some induced infiltration from the pond into the wells.  It is unusual
for such an urbanized community to supply the majority of its water through local sources
and strong measures are needed to ensure that these wells are protected.
Local officials and others note severe algae problems in the pond and poor water quality
in at least some of the five tributaries that flow into Horn Pond, particularly Town Meadow
Brook.  There is one large storm water outfall which drains much of the city center and
discharges directly into the pond.  The Mystic River Watershed Association has indicated
that phosphates and nitrates are excessive in Horn Pond which leads to algae blooms and
cyanobacteria.  The Woburn DPW installed a small bubble diffuser system along the
southerly edge of the pond to reduce biochemical oxygen demand and increase dissolved
oxygen within the pond.  Data to date indicates that the pond system has reduced the
nutrient load and expansion of the aeration system is planned to take place in 2023.

The City, through the MS4 program, has mapped approximately 98% of the municipal
drains and has performed dry weather testing in an effort to identify illicit connections to
the drainage system.  There are 10 tributary areas that have been identified for more
detailed testing and investigation for the removal of illicit connections.  The Woburn DPW
is currently working with a consultant to address the new requirements associated with the
next MS4 permit which was issued in 2016.
2. Water Quality in the Aberjona River - The Massachusetts Surface Water Quality
Standards define six water use classes for surface waters.  Each class designates multiple
water uses for which the water quality shall be suitable.  The Aberjona River is Class B
which has the following uses: fish consumption, aquatic life, primary contact recreation,
secondary contact recreation, aesthetics, non-degradation, agricultural supply, industrial
supply and treated public supply.  Surface waters are monitored to determine if the water
is meeting the standards.  According to the 1992 Commonwealth of Massachusetts
Summary of Water Quality the Aberjona River was classified as "Non-support" meaning
that one or more of the uses was not supported.  The causes of the water quality problem
were found to be unionized ammonia, organic enrichment/dissolved oxygen and
pathogens.  The sources of these pollutants were municipal point sources, urban runoff
and storm sewers.
3. Flooding - Flood hazards as identified in the Federal Emergency Management Agency
(FEMA) and Flood Insurance Rate Maps 1980 (FIRM) as well as the revised 2005 Draft
Flood Study divides the areas into zones, these zones, (A, B, and C) determine the
potential impact to flooding whereas zones A and B are most likely to have flooding issues
in a major rain event and Zone C is an area that is least likely to have flooding.
The primary water body in the city is Horn Pond.  It has a controlled outlet structure which
discharges into the Aberjona River and then flows directly into the Town of Winchester.
In severe storm events water will over top the emergency spillway increasing flow
downstream.  Water also overtops the roadway causing flooding of nearby houses and
apartment complexes and closes off the local roadway into Winchester.  In the event of a
dam failure, there would be catastrophic flooding of downstream areas.
Another area of concern is the Halls Brook Holding area located in the northeast section of
the city on Commerce Way.  This area is prone to flooding in severe conditions, resulting
in closing down the north and south bound lanes and the Commerce Way interchange
from Interstate 93.
Localized flooding occurs throughout the city resulting in flooding of local streets and
properties and road closures.  Improvements have been made to help alleviate areas of
flooding; these mitigation measures include stream maintenance, resized culverts and

drainage lines.  These areas include the Staples building on Washington Street, the
Richard Circle neighborhood, and Four Corners (Cambridge Road and Russell Street).
D. Vegetation
Woburn lies within the Northern Hardwood/Eastern Oak-Hickory forest region.  The upland
forests in this region consist mainly of Oaks, Hickories, Basswood, Maples, Elms, Poplars
and Walnuts.  There is also a well-developed understory often composed of Dogwoods,
Witch Hazel, Blueberries, Huckleberries, Mountain Laurel and Hackberry.  The herbaceous
layer is characterized by a variety of ferns, grasses and wildflowers.
The wetland forests and woodland swamps of Woburn are dominated by Red Maple and
Ashes.  In deciduous woodlands such as those along the northern part of Shaker Glen, the
Atlantic White Cedar, Larch and Hemlock can be found.  The dominant understory trees and
shrubs are Black Chokeberry, Sweet Pepperbush, Dogwoods, Black Alder, Maleberry,
Swamp Azalea, Blueberry and Arrowood.
Public Shade Trees
The City currently spends about $235,000 a year maintaining existing street trees and
planting new ones.  However, the vast majority of the funding is spent on maintenance
activities and not on planting new trees.  The City does routinely install trees along the
frontage of its parks when renovating them, and while they may not technically be street
trees they effectively act as such.  Ferullo Field and Clapp Park are two examples.
The City's Planning Board has required street trees in new subdivisions for decades.  The
trees are located within the roadway rights of way and are maintained either by the City or
by homeowners associations if the roads are not public.
Recognizing the environmental and aesthetic benefits of street trees, the City recently
engaged a consultant to develop a comprehensive street tree planting and maintenance
plan.  Expected to be completed in September of 2023, the plan will include inventories of
existing street trees and locations where plantings are needed, as well as best practices for
selecting, siting, planting, and maintaining trees in the future.  The City's administration has
committed to spending at least $250,000 a year for at least the next 5 years to begin
implementing the plan immediately.  At least $75,000 of those funds will be dedicated to the
purchase and installation of trees.  The City intends to leverage grant resources wherever
possible to augment local funds, and in fact has already partnered with the Mystic River
Watershed Association on a pending $250,000 USDA Forest Service grant that would fund
installation of trees, including City streets, with a focus on locations in environmental justice
areas.

E. Fisheries and Wildlife
BioMap 2 - The Massachusetts Department of Fish & Game, through the Division of
Fisheries and Wildlife's Natural Heritage and Endangered Species Program (NHESP), and
the Nature Conservancy's Massachusetts Program developed BioMap 2 to protect the
state's biodiversity in the context of climate change.  Protection and stewardship of
BioMap 2 Core Habitat and Critical Natural Landscape is considered critical to safeguard
the diversity of species.  The BioMap 2 report for Woburn can be found at
https://www.mass.gov/service-details/biomap2-town-reports
According to this report there are 358 acres of Core Habitat in Woburn but only 230 acres
or 64.2% of that area is protected.  There are also 25 acres of Critical Natural Landscape
of which 24 acres is protected.
The Massachusetts Department of Fisheries stocks Horn Pond several times a year with
trout and bass. The Atlantic Herring have been reaching Horn Pond as a result of a fish
ladder constructed at the dam in Winchester. To assist the Herring being able to enter
Horn Pond to spawn, the City is designing a fish passageway to bypass the Horn Pond
dam. This project is scheduled for construction in the summer of 2024.
Wildlife exists throughout the city and includes coyote, fox, deer, racoons, beaver, skunks
and wild turkeys. Wildlife thrives along the Shaker Glenn Reservation, Horn Pond and the
wooded and marshland areas of West Woburn, the Cranberry Bog and Halls Brook. The
Eversource transmission right of ways also provide important corridors for wildlife.

F. Scenic Resources and Unique Environments
Although Woburn is a densely developed community it has a good number of both historic
and natural features that preserve its history and landscape.  It includes scenic vistas of
the Boston skyline as well as historic structures and monuments.  These scenic resources
are shown on Figure 5.
1. Scenic landscapes
Woburn does not have any landscapes designated as scenic according to the
Massachusetts Landscape Inventory:  A Survey of the Commonwealth's Scenic Areas,
1982.  There are excellent views of downtown Woburn and the surrounding communities
from high points such as Rag Rock.
2. Major Characteristics or Unusual Geologic Features
Glacial activity formed many of the moderate hills and valleys characteristic of Woburn's
landscape. One of the City's most notable features, Horn Pond, a 102-acre pond located
on the Aberjona River, is a product of the glacial period and now serves as a major
recreation area for the City.
Figure 4 shows the soil and geologic features in Woburn. Most of the City is characterized
by the fine sandy loam soil type, described in more detail above. An area of granite
bedrock spans the southeastern corner of the City.
3.  Cultural, archeological and historic areas
The First Burial Ground - The First Burial Ground is located on Park Street.  It was used as
the town burial yard from 1642 until 1794.  The earliest stone is dated 1690.  Daniel
Thompson and Asahel Porter, casualties of the Battles of Lexington and Concord, are
interred here.  Porter was the first to fall in the American Revolution.  The Baldwin family
tomb, marked by a granite obelisk, contains the remains of Colonel Loammi Baldwin and
numerous descendants.
The Second Burial Ground - The Second Burial Ground, located on Montvale Avenue,
dates from 1704 to 1845.  Fifty-one Revolutionary War veterans are buried here.  Many
important early Woburn citizens including Samuel Thompson, Sylvannus Plympton and
others, are buried here.
Baldwin Mansion - The Baldwin Mansion, located at 2 Alfred Street, is on the National
Register of Historic Places.  It was built in 1661 by Deacon Henry Baldwin and altered to
its present appearance by his great grandson, Colonel Loammi Baldwin, in 1803.  Colonel
Baldwin was the builder of the Middlesex Canal, the father of the noted Baldwin apple, and
a Revolutionary War patriot and soldier.  His son, Loammi 2nd, is called the "Father of

American Civil Engineering," and was responsible for the construction of the first naval
drydocks in the western hemisphere.  The Colonel's other sons also had careers in civil
engineering. The property is located within the City's local historic district which means the
building's exterior facades are reasonably protected.
The Rumford House - The Rumford House at 90 Elm Street, is on the national Register of
Historic Places and is a National Historic Landmark.  A National Historic Landmark is a
property of outstanding national significance designated directly by the Department of the
Interior.  Young Benjamin Thomson, alter known as Count Rumford, left Woburn at the age
of 13 to apprentice for a merchant in Salem, but it was here through his friendship with
Loammi Baldwin and their mutual studies at Harvard that his early interest in science was
formed.  Sir Benjamin Thomson, Count Rumford, became a world-renowned soldier,
statesman, inventor and scientist.  The Rumford Historical Association has maintained
Rumford's birthplace at 90 Elm Street as an historic site.  It contains models of his
experiments and inventions, a collection of portraits, and a library of Rumford biographies
and essays.
Battle Road Conservation Area - Woburn sent 180 men, better than half of the available
male population of 311, to join the Lexington-Concord battle of April 19, 1775.  Most of
them reached the battle scene over Battle Road, a wide path still existing in West Woburn.
Over this road went Sylvannus Wood who captured the first Redcoat.  Asahel Porter and
Daniel Thompson, the two Woburn men who were killed by British that day, also used the
road.  The Battle Road runs roughly parallel with Russell Street into Lexington.
The 1790 House - This property is also on the National Register of Historic Places.  This
magnificent home located at 827 Main Street in North Woburn was originally built in 1790
for Woburn lawyer Joseph Bartlett.  Upon completion, however, Baldwin purchased it for
his friend Rumford who had dreams of returning here.  Though these dreams were never
realized, author Frances Parkinson Keys, a frequent guest and visitor of the house, refers
to it repeatedly in his memoirs, "Roses in December", as the "Count Rumford House".
Because of its grand design and pleasant setting it was frequently used for soirees and
balls commemorating important events in Woburn.  In 1800 it was the scene of a Grand
Centennial Ball and in 1803 a gala was held to celebrate the opening of the Middlesex
Canal.
Middlesex Canal - In 1793 an organization was formed to construct the first and longest
towpath canal in U.S. History.  Digging began in 1794 and the canal was completed and
opened from Lowell through Woburn to Boston in 1803.  By 1853 through traffic on the
canal had stopped and in 1859 the corporation was dissolved.  It is fitting that the first
recognizable parts of the canal still in existence north of Boston, starts in Woburn, the
home of the originator and chief builder Loammi Baldwin.  Starting at Kilby Street it

proceeds north to Merrimack Street.  One of the last water bearing remnants of the old
canal is also found in Woburn.  A portion of the canal at the corner of Alfred and Main
Streets, is on the National Register.
Horn Pond Area - The natives referred to Horn Pond as Lake Innitou.  From earliest times
it was a center of recreation and economic activities.  Fishing and ice harvesting were
major attractions.  With the building of the Middlesex Canal, the area commanded the
canal's commercial and social life.  It was a favorite vacation site for residents of Boston
and became one of the first major resort areas in the nation.  The Horn Pond House, built
in 1801, was a thriving hotel and tavern with bowling alleys, restaurant and a ballroom
housed in a magnificent pavilion.  The pump station at the south end of the pond houses a
1903 Pratt iron pump, the only one of its kind made.
Goodyear Green - Goodyear Green is located at the corner of Montvale, Center and
Orange Streets in East Woburn.  In 1839, Charles Goodyear accidentally discovered the
process for the vulcanization of rubber when he dropped a specimen of rubber and sulfur
on a hot stove.  His home was near this location.  Goodyear's discovery made fortunes for
other people, but nothing for him, as he was jailed for debt and later died in poverty.  A
bronze marker on the Green commemorates Goodyear's discovery.
First Congregational Church - This church, located at 322 Main Street, is also on the
National Register of Historic Places.  The first Church in Woburn was established on
August 24, 1642 by a commission of seven from the Charlestown Church.  Headed by
Captain Edward Johnson, the Commission was a part of a committee of thirteen charged
by Charlestown to locate a village on its northern border in 1640.  The village known as
Charlestown Village was incorporated as Wooborne Town on October 7, 1642.  The
present church is the sixth meeting house, built in 1860 by John Stevens, a local architect.
His designs were used to build numerous churches and buildings in New England and in
various other sections of the country.  The building is the tallest wood structure of its kind
in the world.  The main sanctuary is the largest built by wood without internal supports in
the Americas.  The close relationship of the church and town existed even in 1860.  In
constructing the present building, special doors were installed on the north side to
accommodate town council meetings.
The Library - This library, located on Pleasant Street, is on the National Register of Historic
Places and is designated a National Historic Landmark.  There was a Preservation
Restriction that expired in 1996.  The noted architect Henry Hobson Richardson, who also
designed Boston's Trinity Church in Copley Square, created the distinctive design of the
Public Library was one of the first town libraries in the country to be built on such a grand
scale.  A gift of Jonathan Bowers Winn through the bequest of his son, Charles Bowers
Winn to the town of Woburn, the library is still recognized today as one of the superb
architectural landmarks of New England.

U.S. Post Office - The Woburn Center Station at 2 Abbott Street, in Woburn Square, is on
the National Register of Historic Places.
4. Unique Environments
Woburn does not have any areas designated by the state as "Areas of Critical
Environmental Concern".
G. Environmental Challenges
1. Hazardous Waste Sites
As with most densely developed communities with an industrial history, Woburn has a
number of hazardous waste disposal sites.  Most of these sites are considered non-priority
by DEP and are being cleaned up by the private sector under Chapter 21E of the
Massachusetts General Laws.  There are currently 387 sites on this list with many of them
being gas stations or businesses.  There are five Tier 1 sites located in Woburn according
to the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection's (DEP) list of disposal
sites. These include the following:
• Industri Plex 128 on Commerce Way
• 1071 Main Street
• DS Service Center on 482 Washington Street
• Chute Oil Company Facility on 31 High Street
• Dole and Bailey on 16 Conn Street
This list published yearly, identifies the highest priority sites whereas a release of oil or
hazardous materials has been reported to DEP. Tier 1 sites are those that pose the
highest potential risk to people and the environment.  DEP's top priority is to ensure that
unacceptable risks from these sites are eliminated.
Industri-Plex - The major hazardous waste site in Woburn is the Industri-Plex site located
in northeastern Woburn.  This site is on the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency)
Superfund list.  Industri-Plex is a 245 acre industrial site.  From 1853 to 1931 the site was
used to manufacture chemicals for local industries.  From the 1930's to 1969, the site was
used to manufacture glue from animal hides.  The waste from this manufacturing caused
the soils to become contaminated with metals such as arsenic, lead and chrome.  It was
found that the hide piles and lagoons on the site where leaching toxic metals into the
environment.  The groundwater was found to be contaminated with volatile organic
compounds.
In 1986 the EPA selected a site cleanup remedy that started in 1989 and has now been
completed.  Remediation included the design and construction of a permeable cap over
105 acres of contaminated soil, groundwater treatment and the implementation of

institutional controls that restrict future land use.  Redevelopment of the site has in fact
occurred, and included construction of the Regional Transportation Center as well as
some commercial development.
Wells G & H - Wells G & H were two municipal wells developed in 1964 and 1967 to
supplement the water supply of the City of Woburn.  In 1979 contamination in the form of
volatile organic compounds was detected in the wells and they were shut down.  Five
separate properties were found to be the contributing sources of contamination to the
aquifer that supplied the water to these two wells.  The site covers a total area of 330 acres
and the Aberjona River flows through the middle of the site.  The EPA's selected remedy
included excavating and incinerating 2,100 cubic yards of contaminated soils on site and
backfilling the excavated areas; treating additional contaminated soil in place by extracting
soil vapors for treatment and pumping contaminated groundwater from the five source
areas and removing the contaminants for treatment.  The removal and treatment of
contaminated materials and the fencing of one portion of the Wells G&H site reduced the
potential for exposure to hazardous materials at the site while final cleanup activities were
being conducted.  Thirty years later, the EPA and responsible parties are now moving
forward with final wetland restoration around the wells.
2. Landfills
The City's municipal landfill is located on Merrimac Street in North Woburn.  The landfill
has been fenced off, closed and capped, wetlands restoration has been completed and a
gas collection system has been put in place.  The landfill is comprised of 37 acres.  In the
late 1990's the City considered using the landfill for a golf driving range but rejected the
notion given the site's location and potential difficulties marketing the site to a potential
owner/operator.  The City is now exploring the possibility of reusing the site for a solar
field.  A draft request for Proposals is currently being reviewed by the State's Department
of Energy Resources. The City also owns additional land adjacent to the landfill which is
not fenced off. If this area is not needed for the solar installation, its use for passive
recreation should be explored.
3. Erosion
There are no areas in the City where erosion is a serious problem.  Most erosion is temporary
and is related to construction activities.
4. Chronic Flooding
There is a problem with flooding along the Middlesex Canal in the vicinity of Hart Street.
This flooding affects about 30 homes that abut the Middlesex Canal.  Information on
efforts to address this flooding can be found on page 46.
5. Sedimentation
Sedimentation is not a major problem in the city.  There is some sedimentation related to
construction activities but these impacts are usually temporary.

6. New Development
Woburn is a densely developed suburb with a large employment base due to its excellent
highway access.  The high points in the city such as Rag Rock conservation area afford
sweeping views of a variety of landscapes including the Boston skyline.  The impact of
additional development will be felt most strongly in the southwestern portion of the city as
the demand for residential development continues.  Increased development will place a
greater strain on municipal services including schools, police, fire as well as on the water
supply.  It will also impact wildlife habitat areas as fewer large open parcels remain.
Increased development also means an increase in paved areas (impervious surfaces)
which can increase stormwater runoff, pollution and flooding.
7. Ground and surface water pollution: point and non-point
Woburn obtains approximately 65% of its water supply from the Horn Pond aquifer through
5 municipal wells situated on the westerly side of the pond.  The Aberjona aquifer has not
been used since 1978 when TCE was discovered in Wells G and H and these wells were
abandoned at that time.  Groundwater supplies are typically high in iron and manganese
and the City commissioned a new ground water filtration plant for this purpose in 2012.
The facility removes 99.9% of the iron and manganese from the groundwater thus
eliminating previous problems with discolored water.
8. Impaired Water Bodies
Water Quality in Horn Pond - Local officials and others note algae problems in Horn Pond
and poor water quality in at least some of the five tributaries that flow into Horn Pond,
particularly Town Meadow Brook.  There is one large stormwater outfall that discharges
directly into the pond and which drains much of the city center.  The pond is also
impacted by surcharging of an MWRA sewer trunk line during severe wet weather that
causes a sewer system overflow near Sturgis Street adjacent to the pond.  The City of
Woburn through a five year infiltration/inflow capital improvements program has reduced
the frequency and duration of this overflow substantially and the SSO is triggered only
when the MWRA trunk line surcharges.  The primary pathway for potential human
exposure to pollutants in the pond is the consumption of fish.
Water Quality in the Aberjona River - The Massachusetts Surface Water Quality Standards
define six water use classes for surface waters.  Each class designates multiple water
uses for which the water quality shall be suitable.  The Aberjona River is Class B which has
the following uses: fish consumption, aquatic life, primary contact recreation, secondary
contact recreation, aesthetics, non-degradation, agricultural supply, industrial supply and
treated public supply.  Surface waters are monitored to determine if the water is meeting
the standards.
Water quality information for the Aberjona River can be found in the EPA's Mystic River
Watershed Report Card, most recently updated in 2021, which is based on ongoing data
collection by the Mystic River Watershed Association (MyRWA).  The segment of the

Aberjona River that flows through Woburn is on the 1998 303(d) list of impaired waters due
to ammonia, organic enrichment/low dissolved oxygen and pathogens.
According to that report, the lower 6.6 miles of the Aberjona River are in non-support of
aquatic life standards due to organic enrichment, low dissolved oxygen and other habitat
alterations.  The river has not been assessed for fish consumption and is in non-support of
primary contact recreation standards because of pathogens from illicit sewer connections
and waterfowl waste.  The river is in support of secondary contact recreation and aesthetic
standards.
MyRWA concluded that urban runoff impacts the water quality of both Horn Pond and the
Aberjona River, contributing to elevated levels of E. coli, total phosphorus and nitrogen.
Additionally, high levels of cyanobacteria blooms have occurred in Horn Pond in recent
years.  The City installed a small bubble diffuser system in 2012 to increase the dissolved
oxygen in Horn Pond to address the high nutrient loadings and algae blooms.  Additional
aeration facilities are planned for the pond.
In conjunction with the City's MS4 permit, approximately 96% of the municipal drainage
system and outfalls have been mapped and ten drainage areas have been found to have
elevated levels of surfactants and bacteria.  The City is developing a program to locate
and eliminate these illicit connections in anticipation of the new MS4 permit.
9. Invasive species
Many invasive plant species are commonly found throughout Woburn.  These include
purple loosestrife, honeysuckle, phragmites, Oriental bittersweet, barberry, buckthorn,
Japanese knotweed and Norway maple.  Where found, these species can crowd out
native plants to the extent they either negatively affect localized ecosystems or interfere
with use of trails and some open spaces.
The City has undertaken several initiatives to deal with the issue of invasive species.  The
City has hired crews to clear specific environmentally-sensitive areas of invasive plants by
hand to address a particularly problematic area.  On an on-going basis, citizen volunteers
conduct hand-clearing of invasive plants during the City's annual Conservation Day
activities and occasionally on other days throughout the year.  To date most of these
volunteer efforts have been focused on the Horn Pond recreational facility, but other
parcels have also been the subject of targeted clearing efforts.
10. Environmental Equity Issues
Environmental Justice and the Distribution of Parks and Open Spaces
The Environmental Protection Agency defines Environmental Justice (EJ) as fair treatment
and meaningful involvement of all people regardless of race, color, national origin, or

income, with respect to the development, implementation, and enforcement of
environmental laws, regulations, and policies. To this end, the City of Woburn and other
responsible parties have addressed and/or plan to address several environmental
challenges that impact EJ communities. Environmental challenges being addressed within
the city's EJ communities include hazardous waste sites, landfills, chronic flooding, and
impaired waterbodies.
While this perspective primarily highlights inequitable distribution of exposure to
environmental harm, EJ communities also refer to the equitable distribution of
environmental benefits, such as access to natural resources, parks, open spaces and
recreational resources.  Massachusetts currently uses 2020 ACS data to define
Environmental Justice Populations1 by U.S. Census block group as shown in Figure 2:
Environmental Justice Populations.  This map illustrates the location of EJ populations
mostly in the northeastern and central areas of the city, with a small swath of the city near
Whispering Hill just west of the soccer complex.  This figure also illustrates that parks are
relatively well distributed throughout the city and EJ communities.  A few gaps in access
and distribution remain, and should be considered a priority for investment:
• the northeast area of the city (north of MA RT 128 and east of New Boston St).  The
lack of green space in this area could be due to it's industrial zoning designation.
Even so, the acquisition of parkland in this area should be considered.
• The far east area of the city just south of MA RT 128 and Walnut Hill.  This area is

11. Accessibility
Accessibility Requirements - The Open Space and Recreation Planner's Workbook states
that all municipal property and programs must be accessible to people with disabilities.
Furthermore, all municipal park and conservation areas and programs must be evaluated
as part of the process of preparing an open space and recreation plan.  This section gives
an overview of accessibility issues in Woburn.  The complete facilities inventory and
transition plan is contained in Appendix C along with the administrative requirements.

Commission on Disability - The Woburn Commission on Disability is a volunteer group that
aids in answering questions and serving the needs of the disabled community in the City
of Woburn.  The Commission meets virtually on a monthly basis at City Hall and meetings
are open to the public.
Physical facilities - It can be difficult to determine what standards apply because the
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), the Architectural Access Board (AAB) and DCR all
have different standards. Many of the playgrounds and tot lots utilize a wood chip surface.
Wood chips are considered acceptable by the ADA and AAB but they are not ideal for a
number of reasons and must be maintained.  Proper maintenance in the form of leveling
and smoothing is required to maintain the proper ground height at access transfer
platforms.  People with small children also noted that toddlers and young children are
prone to putting the wood chips in their mouths and that sharp objects and other foreign
material can become trapped under the chips and thereby, posing a safety hazard.
Program evaluation -The Recreation Department offers several programs for children and
young adults with disabilities now called Adaptive Recreation programs.  The Recreation
Department has expanded their program offerings for Adaptive Recreation over the past
few years.  We currently have Social Clubs, Movie Nights, Field Trips to local spots,
swimming, bowling, walking clubs, basketball and more programs are added as each year
goes on. Recently the Recreation Department hired an adaptive program coordinator to
begin outreach to start new programs for children and adults with disabilities.
Various youth organizations offer challenger programs, i.e. Little League offers Challenger
Baseball, Woburn Youth Hockey offers Challenger Hockey and Woburn Youth Soccer
offers Challenger Soccer.  In addition, the Recreation Department collaborates with the
Burlington Recreation Department to offer a program for adults with disabilities.
The Recreation Department reports that the programs for children with disabilities are wellattended and that children with disabilities also participate in their general programs.  The
Department is always willing to make reasonable accommodations to facilitate
participation by any child with a disability.  The staff summer orientation includes
information on how to accommodate residents with a disability.  The Recreation
Department finds that the main reason why people are not registering is due to lack of
transportation.  The Recreation Department is hoping to do more outreach in the future
with the School Department to offer more programs after school and to collaborate with
transportation.

SECTION V:  INVENTORY OF LANDS OF CONSERVATION AND
RECREATION INTEREST
A. Introduction
Open space and recreation resources in the City of Woburn encompass a variety of types
of land and water sites, as well as cultural and historic resources, both publicly and
privately owned. Open space includes parks, active recreation fields, playgrounds,
conservation lands, woodlands, greenways, bike paths, and any other properties that
might provide recreational value to surrounding neighborhoods.
Uses of open space range from passive (and often informal) recreational uses such as
walking, hiking, jogging, fishing, bathing, boating, and picnicking, to active recreation such
as field-based sports, court games, playgrounds, aquatic parks and other built facilities or
amenities that require more formalized and often intensive development and
management. Passive recreation might also be referred to as "low intensity recreation" as
it usually relies less on built facilities and is often associated with conservation lands.
Therefore, passive uses are typically closely aligned with the goals of preserving natural
resources and natural habitats.
The protection of open space and recreation resources is vital to the health of both the
residents of Woburn and also their environment. Access to parks and open space is
proven to improve mental and physical health, strengthen a sense of community, benefit
the local economy, and enhance the natural environment.
Appendix B is a listing of all lands of conservation and recreation interest. One purpose of
the inventory is to evaluate the current levels of protection for open space and recreation
resources. For planning purposes, it is important to be aware of the degree of protection
for each parcel.  Knowing the level of protection (or lack thereof) will point out how easily
some properties assumed to be open space can be developed.  This knowledge will help
identify open space and recreation areas that need additional effort for their preservation
and protection.
The second purpose of this inventory is to make the reader aware of the open spaces that
exist in the city and to provide a baseline against which to evaluate existing and future
needs. Cataloging lands of open space and recreation interest allows the City to take
stock of current resources and compare them against demographic trends to plan for
residents' recreation needs in the future. More information can be found in Section VII
Analysis of Needs.

B. Definitions and Categories
The classification for protection status used in this plan comes from MassGIS: Protected
and Recreational Open Space data layer. The data layer classifies each parcel Protection
Level as In Perpetuity, Temporary, Limited or None, see Appendix B for specific definitions
for each Level of Protection.  The inventory does not reflect any additional research into
deeds, restrictions or municipal votes and will need to be updated if new information is
discovered about these parcels.
The inventory is divided into seven categories based on ownership and use:
City owned Conservation Lands
There are 333.06 acres of conservation lands in Woburn, 4.0% of the total city area
(8,281.6 acres/12.94 sq miles), which is managed by the Conservation Commission.
Recreation within these parcels is typically hiking/walking. The primary purpose for
some parcels is environmental protection and as such are largely unimproved.
City Owned Recreation Lands
There are 182.12 acres of public owned open space and recreation land, 2.2% of the
total acreage of the city, that is managed by the Parks and Recreation Department.
These properties are largely athletic fields, parks and playgrounds.
Other City Lands
There are 127.71 acres of land (1.5% of city) that are managed by other city agencies
or the managing agency is not identified.
School Facilities
There are 55.6 acres of school land (0.7% of City area) that provides recreation
facilities, typically athletic fields and playgrounds.
Private Protected Lands
There are 82.01 acres of private land  (1.0% of City area) under varying degrees of
protection. These are largely cemeteries and private parcels with conservation
easements.
Chapter 61 Lands
There are two parcels totaling 36.3 acres of land assessed under Chapter 61. The
Mahoney's parcel (16.7 acres) is assessed as horticultural land.  The 19.6 acre Mass.
Rifle Association parcel is assessed as recreation.  The City has the right of first
refusal on these parcels.

Other Parcels of Recreation or Conservation Interest
There are 267.17 acres of land of recreation or conservation interest (3.2% of City
area) which are either not owned by the City or are owned by the City but are not
open to the general public:
Cummings Property - The City of Boston owns property in Burlington and Woburn.
The main parcel is adjacent to the Burlington campus of Northeastern University.
There are several non-contiguous parcels.  The Woburn portion of the Cummings
Property is approximately 46 acres.  This property was deeded to the City by Mary
Cummings in the 1920's with the stipulation that it be used to create a public
pleasure ground for the poor of Boston.  The city entered into an agreement with
the Trustees of Reservations to manage the property. The three non-contiguous
parcels were to provide income for the upkeep of the main parcel and could be
sold to benefit the main parcel.  The sale or conversion of the main parcel would be
subject to Article 97 of the state constitution.
City of Boston land at Willow and Locust - This parcel is adjacent to a school and
includes wetlands.
Horn Pond - This property, the location for the Woburn Country Club, is owned by
the City and managed by the Woburn Golf and Ski Authority which is a nine member
board appointed by the Mayor and approved by the City Council. The Authority is
responsible for overseeing, maintaining and operating the Woburn Country Club as
established by Chapter 526 of the acts of 1968 of the General Laws. The country club
is not open to the general public and use of the golf course requires a paid
membership.
Winchester Elks - This parcel is adjacent to Horn Pond Mountain and contains
wetlands and rare vegetation.  It is also within the Zone II of a municipal well.

B. Statement of Open Space and Recreation Goals
Woburn is a community with significant natural resources, open spaces, and recreation
facilities, and during the public process residents consistently emphasized the importance
of keeping up with maintenance of existing facilities, creating multi-generational recreation
opportunities, and expanding both active and passive recreational facilities. Therefore, the
City's goals are to maintain, update, and expand on existing resources as open spaces
and recreation facilities are essential for the continued health and well-being of the
environment and all of its residents.
