SECTION VII:  ANALYSIS OF NEEDS
A. Summary of Resource Protection Needs
The primary resource protection need in Woburn is protection of the water supply.  The city
gets 63% of its water supply from groundwater and has already experienced the impact of
losing a portion of its water supply due to pollution.  Therefore, protection efforts in the
Horn Pond watershed including the acquisition of additional land, is a critical need.  The
Natural Heritage and Endangered Species Program also identified Horn Pond as a priority
habitat area in need of further protection.
B. Community Meeting Feedback and Online Survey Results
Feedback from Workshop 1 and Workshop 1A was used to identify additional recreational
needs for the city. These workshops were held on September 15, 2022 and September 22,
2022 at the Woburn Public Library. Participants provided input on Woburn's needs, which
were written on large boards in front of the group. Following the discussion, participants
were given sticker dots to vote on their most important items. Key themes were:
• Increase passive recreation
• Offer multi-generational opportunities that address the needs of various age groups
from children to seniors
• Improve maintenance
• Improve universal accessibility
• Improve/increase amenities at existing facilities
• Encourage stewardship / awareness of open space as a shared resource
• Strategic planning (make use of underutilized areas as potential recreation
opportunities, design open spaces as a system, acquire parcels adjacent to key
open space areas)

D. Management Needs, Potential Change of Use
Currently, there are certain parks and parcels of open space (in particular Horn Pond), that
are well-known and heavily used, while other conservation land and recreational areas are
under-utilized.  The Conservation Commission has stressed the need to inform and
encourage residents to use these other less known areas, in order to reduce the negative
impacts of overuse on facilities like Horn Pond.  There is also a need to provide better
access to some conservation areas and parks, particularly with respect to universal
access. Public meeting comments and online survey results indicate that maintenance of
Woburn's open spaces is a critical need.
E. Analysis of Woburn's Demographics
Demographic trends over the past decade and population projections described in
Section III anticipate an increase in persons 70-85 relative to other age groups. Based on
this trend, Woburn will need to plan for an increasing older adult population by offering
recreational opportunities that serve the population's unique needs.  According to the
National Parks and Recreation Agency, programs and services offered through parks and
recreation address the diverse health and wellness needs of the growing older adult
populations.   Chronic disease prevention and management, improved access to healthy

foods and increased opportunities to establish strong and healthy social connections can
enhance the health and wellbeing of older adult populations.
When developing programs and services for active adults, three levels of intensity should
be offered:  Low, moderate and high.  Low intensity is intended for older adults who may
require therapeutic recreational services where high intensity activities such as fitness
classes, golf, tennis and swimming are more suitable for active adults with few disabilities
or chronic disease.
Based on the results of a comprehensive community engagement process, older adults in
Woburn see a need for multi-generational facilities, new and improved walking trails, and
pickle ball courts.  One senior requested a playground at the senior center so their
grandchildren had a space to play while visiting.  Finally, several older adults requested
community garden plots, which could improve access to healthy foods while providing a
therapeutic, nature-based activity.
The needs of residents with disabilities also vary.  Some residents with disabilities can
participate in regular recreational programs without any modifications while others may
need some assistance.  Depending on the degree of disability, there may also be a need
for specific programs geared for that population. Physical barriers are a key factor and will
need to be evaluated through the Section 504 process and eliminated in a systematic
fashion.
Teens are another demographic often requiring more focused attention to garner input
regarding recreation needs and wants. Teens are one the more difficult populations to
engage and retain as users of public parks and recreation programs and services.
Currently, the City does have seasonal recreation programs targeted at teens. Winter
programs have been successful, but there are few registrants for the summer programs,
indicating the City may want to consider retire those programs or gain a deeper
understanding of barriers to participation. The City has identified one capital project
specific to primarily teens:  a skatepark.  There is a completed design for the skatepark,
and it is on the capital improvement list for funding and implementation.
While specific feedback from teens was not received to inform the recommendations of
this plan, the city, through its Recreation Department and Commission, plans to undergo
more targeted outreach to identify teen recreation needs and wants, and barriers to use
and participation.  Additional feedback will enable the City to make informed decisions
regarding investment in teen-focused facilities, programs and services.

F. SCORP findings
The SCORP (Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan) is the state's equivalent
of a municipal open space plan.  SCORP plans are developed by individual states to be
eligible for federal Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) grants.  The current plan is
called "Massachusetts Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan 2017".
The SCORP plan surveyed Massachusetts residents through a telephone survey, youth
survey and public meetings.  A few of the key findings are below that align with community
feedback from the public workshops and online survey.
• Running, walking, and jogging are the top activities reported by adults and youth
which aligns with the results of the online survey.
• Both youths and adults in the state want more trails and water-based facilities.
• At the local level, improvements to water-based recreation facilities top residents'
priorities, followed by playgrounds and other park-type amenities.
The state's SCORP also notes two key findings related to Woburn's demographic trends:
• Over 46% of residents older than 75 identified as having a disability.
For people with disabilities, getting to facilities to recreate is quite difficult as public
transportation is often not reliable for them.
• 11.7% of Massachusetts residents self-identified as having a disability, with the
majority of them being ambulatory.
These findings suggest that the increase in persons age 70-85 may be correlated to an
increase in the disabled population, and the city should plan accordingly.
The following goals outlined in SCORP align with the Goals and Objectives laid out in
Section VIII.
1. Access for Underserved Populations
2. Support the Statewide Trails Initiative
3. Increase the Availability of Water-based Recreation
4. Support the Creation and Renovation of Neighborhood Parks

H. Conclusions
Based on proximity of existing open space and recreation opportunities to existing EJ
block groups as noted in Section III, more recreation investment is needed northwest of
Route 128/I-95.
The most popular active pursuit from the online survey, trails for walking, jogging and
hiking is supported by the SCORP findings. Hiking trails should be maintained/created at
other properties to ease the pressure on Horn Pond given that Horn Pond is important for
the protection of the city's water supply and for wildlife habitat.
The desire for more playgrounds registered in the online survey is supported by the NRPA
data analysis. Additionally, Woburn's Parks and Recreation staffing levels are below average

compared with NRPA metrics which could account for the maintenance concerns being
high on the community's priority list.
The demographics projections in Section III suggest a need to plan for an aging
population. The findings from SCORP note that the elderly population is also likely to be
disabled and likely to have difficulty getting to facilities. Expanding the recreation options
at the Senior Center for frail elderly residents and installing adult fitness stations for more
active residents could address some of these needs. Transportation for the frail elderly to
recreation options should also be addressed.
As noted in Section IV, there is also a need for additional transportation options for
Adaptive Recreation programs. The City should work with the School Department to offer
more Adaptive Recreation programs after school and to collaborate on transportation for
events off school properties.

SECTION VIII:  GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
During the community process described in Section VI Community Vision and Appendix A,
participants at Workshops 1 and 1A provided their feedback desired improvements and
priorities for Woburn's open space and recreation system. This list was combined with
results from the online community survey, outstanding projects remaining from the
previous OSRP and Recreation Commission priorities, and common themes were
identified. These themes were developed into Goals and Objectives that were presented
to participants at Workshop 2 for review and comment. The Goal and Objectives
presented below represent the outcome of that public process.
Goal #1:  Provide Active and Passive Recreational Opportunities for All Residents
Objective #1:  Create multi-use trails to provide access to open spaces and other uses.
Objective #2:  Ensure compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act by undertaking
improvements that improve handicapped accessibility.
Objective #3:  Provide multi-generational recreational facilities  with a particular emphasis
on replacement of playground equipment.
Objective #4:  Provide neighborhood recreational facilities scattered throughout the city.
Goal #2:  Manage Existing Recreation and Conservation Lands for Maximum Benefits
Objective #1:  Secure additional funding for maintenance.
Objective #2:  Acquire parcels adjacent to existing city owned parks and conservation
lands to provide better access and as a buffer from adjacent land uses.
Objective #3:  Increase the use of lesser-known conservation areas to reduce the
pressure on popular areas such as Horn Pond.
Goal #3:  Protect Woburn's Natural Resources
Objective #1:  Provide for the protection of wetlands and water resources through
vigorous enforcement of the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act (310 CMR 10.00) and
other pertinent state and federal regulations.

Objective #2:  Protect Woburn's water supply through enforcement of the groundwater
protection overlay district and selective land acquisitions in the Horn Pond watershed.
Objective #3:  Acquire parcels of land with significant natural resources and wildlife
habitat values.
Goal #4:  Acquire New Open Space Lands
Objective #1:  Acquire lands adjacent to city owned parcels for buffer from other uses and
for parking and access.
Objective #2:  Develop a mechanism to provide the local match required to take
advantage of federal and state grant programs.
Objective #3:  Actively encourage the donation of land through conservation restrictions
and easements.
Goal #5:  Coordinate Local and Regional Open Space Planning Efforts
Objective #1:  Consider the impacts of open space planning decisions on surrounding
communities.
Objective #2:  Take advantage of opportunities to participate in regional open space
initiatives.
Goal #6:  Protect Cultural and Historic Resources
Objective #1:  Use a variety of techniques to protect the City's cultural and historic
resources and implement measures that enhance the public's enjoyment and awareness
of those resources.

SECTION IX - SEVEN-YEAR ACTION PLAN
The Seven Year Action Plan is the most important section in any open space and
recreation plan.  The following recommendations are meant to bridge the gap between the
existing open space and recreation resources identified in Section V, the goals and
objectives (Section VIII) and the needs and desires of the residents of Woburn (Section
VII).  The designation of a target year is meant as a guide only.  It is more important to be
flexible and take advantage of opportunities as they arise.  Certain actions are designated
as ongoing (covering all seven years) because of the flexibility required to pursue a
program of land acquisition or the length of time required to design, engineer, permit and
build a project.

SMART GROWTH AND REGIONAL COLLABORATION
November 1, 2023
Melissa Cryan
Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs
100 Cambridge St. - Suite 900
Boston, MA  02114
Dear Ms. Cryan:
The City of Woburn's 2023-2029 "Open Space and Recreation Plan" was recently submitted
to the Metropolitan Area Planning Council (MAPC) for review.
The Division of Conservation Services (DCS) requires that all open space plans be reviewed
by the applicable regional planning agency. This review is advisory and only DCS has the power
to approve a municipal open space plan. While your office reviews open space plans for
compliance with your guidelines, MAPC reviews these plans for their attention to regional
issues generally and more specifically for consistency with MetroCommon 2050, the regional
policy plan for the Boston metropolitan area.
Consistency with MetroCommon 2050 - MetroCommon 2050 is the official regional plan for
Greater Boston. Adopted in 2021, in accordance with Massachusetts General Law, the plan
seeks to expand equity throughout the region and envisions a more prosperous, resilient, and
sustainable Greater Boston for existing and future residents. This vision is embodied in and
supported by 11 goals, 5 action areas, 20 recommendations, 68 strategies, and over 200
policy actions. We encourage all communities within the MAPC region to become familiar with
the plan by visiting www.metrocommon.mapc.org.
The Woburn OSRP directly references consistency with MetroCommon 2050, and its role in
focusing regional support for our local efforts. The plan emphasizes the City's commitment to
improving its walking and biking network and making parks and open spaces more accessible.
It also stresses the importance of exploring various funding options for park and open space
maintenance including the Community Preservation Act.
Community Preservation Act - The Community Preservation Act (CPA) is a smart growth tool
that helps communities preserve open space and historic sites, develop outdoor recreational
facilities, and create affordable housing. Communities can raise funds through a voterauthorized surcharge on local property tax bills of up to 3%. The state also matches these
funds with annual distributions from the Community Preservation Trust Fund. We note that
Woburn has not adopted the CPA, but we are encouraged to see that the OSRP's
recommended implementation actions include consideration of CPA.

SMART GROWTH AND REGIONAL COLLABORATION
Moreover, the plan aims to balance conservation efforts for wildlife habitat and natural
resources while providing the community with enjoyable recreational opportunities. The not only provides detailed inventory maps of the City's open space resources but also
highlights the importance of regional coordination.
Surrounding Communities - The plan emphasizes the need for collaborative planning with
surrounding communities to create a more cohesive and integrated network of regional open
space and recreational resources. Woburn has multiple significant resources that are shared
with neighboring communities. These include the historic Middlesex Canal, a 27-mile
waterway that once linked Boston to the Merrimack River in Lowell, as well as the TriCommunity Greenway, a 5.7-mile multi-use path that connects portions of Stoneham,
Winchester, and Woburn.
The Woburn Open Space and Recreation Plan is very comprehensive and should serve the
City well as it continues its efforts to preserve open space and provide for the recreational
needs of its residents.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this plan.
Sincerely,

Meeting Minutes:
City of Woburn
Open Space and Recreation Plan Update
Workshop #1
Thursday, September 15, 2022
Woburn Public Library
6:30 - 8:30 pm
City personnel in attendance:  Mayor Scott Galvin, City Engineer Jay Corey, Recreation Director
Rory Lindstrom, Wellness Coordinator Brian Nagle, Planning Director Tina Cassidy, GIS
Coordinator Matt Barrett
Approximately twenty-five (25) residents were in attendance.
Comments/suggestions/recommendations made by the public included the following:
•
Create a recreational site that has outdoor gym equipment at different stations around a
"fitness loop".
•
Expand the "reach" (attractiveness) of the Senior Center to younger generations by adding
other appropriate recreational opportunities there. Specifically, add recreational facilities for
young children at this site.
•
Create more community gardens at sites other than Horn Pond that are universally
accessible.
•
Do more maintenance of open space land.
•
Acquire parcels on "Horn Pond Mountain" that are still in private ownership.
•
Dredge Horn Pond, remove concrete block from dam area, and provide more maintenance
of this heavily-used parcel.
•
Extend the trail in the Shaker Glen conservation area that runs toward Lexington.  Bridges
over the brook are deteriorating and need to be repaired.  There are many felled trees that
should be removed and which could perhaps be re-purposed as wood chips or fuel.   Trail
could be extended via the power lines into Lexington; significant overgrowth needs to be
removed.

•
New trail at former Shannon Farm has associated public parking, and the trail will need to
be maintained in the future.
•
All playgrounds should be "universally" designed in terms of access.
•
Lots of glass and debris in the groundcover of the playground area at Ferullo Field.
•
Add trail (running?) through Whispering Hill Woods.  Connect Whispering Hill to Mary
Cummings Park and Shannon Farm trails.
•
New footbridges and signage are needed at Whispering Hill.
•
The City should create a "master plan" for Horn Pond that is sustainable by the City over
time; there are lots of types of users, and conflicts sometimes between them.  Overall, the
message that Horn Pond is a shared community asset needs to be reinforced.
•
Add more recycling receptacles to Horn Pond and do a more effective public awareness
campaign to encourage recycling.  Oversight and enforcement will be needed, with or
without signage.  Monofilament line used by fishermen is a particular problem.
•
Shaker Glen would be a good spot for more community gardens.
•
The old Tarky School site, which abuts Battle Road, may be an opportunity for passive
recreational uses.
•
The ballfields at Gillis Field are in particular bad shape - they need maintenance.
•
The City's parks and playgrounds are well maintained, passive recreational opportunities
are what is really needed.
•
Benches and solar lights at various locations in Shaker Glen and Horn Pond might increase
activity levels.
•
There is seemingly no management of the woodlands in various forested open space
parcels being done presently.
•
A farmers' market at the Senior Center would be a good idea, as would more community
gardens.  A farmers' market would introduce new people to the Senior Center, to increase
its use.  Involving school-age children at the site would be a good idea too.
•
Make Horn Pond part of the school curriculum so future stewards are created.
•
Having other major recreational sites besides Horn Pond would reduce the pressure on
Horn Pond's facilities.
•
The Plympton School site should be equipped with benches and trees and serve as a
passive recreational space once the school is demolished.
•
Can parking be added at or near the Russell Street soccer field, to avoid the doubleparking problem that currently exists?

City Meeting Minutes:
City of Woburn
Open Space and Recreation Plan Update
Workshop #1a
(Repeat of Workshop #1 held on September 15, 2022, held to
accommodate those who may have had a scheduling conflict the prior week)
Thursday, September 22, 2022
City Council Chambers, City Hall
6:00 - 7:00 pm
City personnel in attendance:  Mayor Scott Galvin, City Engineer Jay Corey, Recreation Director
Rory Lindstrom, Wellness Coordinator Brian Nagle, Planning Director Tina Cassidy, GIS
Coordinator Matt Barrett
Approximately twelve (12) residents were in attendance.
Comments/suggestions/recommendations made by the public included the following:
•
Middlesex Canal:  Great potential for a walking path with benches, signage, historical
markers, etc.  Would connect multiple neighborhoods via an off-road trail and highlight
important part of Woburn's history.
•
Existing community gardens:
*
More plots are needed to meet demand (there is currently a waiting list).
*
Recently installed restroom facilities are great amenity that should be permanent.
*
More parking is needed (though area has wetlands and is in a floodplain so that
complicates ability to expand existing parking area).
*
Access driveway needs work.
*
Site is ideal space to add features that encourage bird nesting.
*
Significant problem with invasive species there - as in many places in Woburn - and
they should be cleaned out.
*
Would be great to have an on-site compost area, a few benches and maybe a picnic
table.
•
There is a need for more community garden space in a different location(s), to serve interest
in different parts of the City.  Is there another suitable location?
•
The Rag Rock site off Harrison Avenue could be improved and used for passive recreation;
invasive species would need to be cleared.

•
Create a way for younger adults to participate in planning future open space and recreation
uses/facilities, in order to develop the next generation of advocates/participants in open
space and recreation initiatives.
•
"Pop-up" gardens (aka "urban guerilla gardens"), created in locations along streets by
intentionally scattering wildflower seeds, would beautify the City.
•
Forest Park should be improved with walking paths and by clearing invasive species and
replacing them with native plantings.
•
Create more off-road bike and walking trails/paths.
•
Establish a committee to focus on trails and paths in a coordinated, City-wide effort, with the
mission of linking the various existing networks in Woburn to each other and to nearby
communities, and implementing a system of coordinated/improved trail markings.
•
Pursue opportunities to fund future maintenance of trails and bikeways, perhaps by seeking
private funding from sponsors willing to donate.
•
There is demand and need for a second dog park, preferably on the City's west side.  The
old Tarky School site and the newest open space parcel to be added to Shaker Glen (the
former Shannon Farm parcel) might be candidate locations.

Definitions of "Level of Protection"
Source: MassGIS Data: Protected and Recreational OpenSpace
In Perpetuity:  Legally protected in perpetuity and recorded as such in a deed or other official document. Land is considered protected in perpetuity if it is owned by
the town's conservation commission or, sometimes, by the water department; if a town has a conservation restriction on the property in perpetuity; if it is owned by one
of the state's conservation agencies (thereby covered by article 97); if it is owned by a non-profit land trust; or if the town received federal or state assistance for the
purchase or improvement of the property. Private land is considered protected if it has a deed restriction in perpetuity, if an Agriculture Preservation Restriction has
been placed on it, or a Conservation Restriction has been placed on it.
Limited:  Protected by legal mechanisms other than those above, or protected through functional or traditional use. These lands might be protected by a requirement
of a majority municipal vote for any change in status. This designation also includes lands that are likely to remain open space for other reasons (e.g. cemeteries and
municipal golf courses).
Temporary:  Legally protected for less than perpetuity (e.g. short term conservation restriction), or temporarily protected through an existing functional use. For
example, some water district lands are only temporarily protected while water resource protection is their primary use. These lands could be developed for other uses
at the end of their temporary protection or when their functional use is no longer necessary. These lands will revert to unprotected status at a given date unless
protection status is extended.

recommendations.text: Goal #1:  Provide Active and Passive Recreational Opportunities for All Residents
Objective #1:  Create multi-use trails to provide access to open spaces and other uses.
Objective #2:  Ensure compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act by undertaking improvements that improve handicapped accessibility.
Objective #3:  Provide multi-generational recreational facilities  with a particular emphasis on replacement of playground equipment.
Objective #4:  Provide neighborhood recreational facilities scattered throughout the city.
Goal #2:  Manage Existing Recreation and Conservation Lands for Maximum Benefits
Objective #1:  Secure additional funding for maintenance.
Objective #2:  Acquire parcels adjacent to existing city owned parks and conservation lands to provide better access and as a buffer from adjacent land uses.
Objective #3:  Increase the use of lesser-known conservation areas to reduce the pressure on popular areas such as Horn Pond.
Goal #3:  Protect Woburn's Natural Resources

Objective #1:  Provide for the protection of wetlands and water resources through vigorous enforcement of the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act (310 CMR 10.00) and other pertinent state and federal regulations.
Objective #2:  Protect Woburn's water supply through enforcement of the groundwater protection overlay district and selective land acquisitions in the Horn Pond watershed.
Objective #3:  Acquire parcels of land with significant natural resources and wildlife habitat values.
Goal #4:  Acquire New Open Space Lands
Objective #1:  Acquire lands adjacent to city owned parcels for buffer from other uses and for parking and access.
Objective #2:  Develop a mechanism to provide the local match required to take advantage of federal and state grant programs.
Objective #3:  Actively encourage the donation of land through conservation restrictions and easements.
Goal #5:  Coordinate Local and Regional Open Space Planning Efforts
Objective #1:  Consider the impacts of open space planning decisions on surrounding communities.
Objective #2:  Take advantage of opportunities to participate in regional open space initiatives.
Goal #6:  Protect Cultural and Historic Resources
Objective #1:  Use a variety of techniques to protect the City's cultural and historic resources and implement measures that enhance the public's enjoyment and awareness of those resources.
